title: Elevated-Temperature Tribo-Corrosion Response of Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy.

recollection.starting_material: Guess: A cast eutectic high-entropy alloy of the Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni family (commonly AlCoCrFeNi2.1), exhibiting a lamellar dual-phase microstructure (FCC + ordered B2), prepared by arc melting and homogenization/polishing prior to testing.
recollection.intervention: Guess: Elevated-temperature tribo-corrosion tests using a ball-on-disk or reciprocating setup in a chloride-containing aqueous electrolyte (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl), at multiple temperatures (approximately 25–90/120 C), combining electrochemical measurements (OCP, potentiodynamic polarization, potentiostatic holds/EIS) with in situ sliding under a normal load (a few N) and set sliding speed/path length.
recollection.structure: Guess: The as-cast lamellar FCC/B2 eutectic is retained; under tribo-corrosion a tribo-oxide film forms comprising Cr2O3-/Al2O3-rich oxides and mixed spinels (e.g., NiCr2O4) with selective dissolution of the Al-rich B2 lamellae, resulting in a surface enriched in Cr/Ni-rich FCC and a patchy oxide glaze within the wear track.
recollection.mechanism: Guess: Temperature-accelerated electrochemical dissolution and repassivation occur concurrently with mechanical film removal. The Al-rich B2 phase acts anodic relative to the FCC, promoting preferential attack (galvanic coupling within the lamellae). At higher temperature, oxide formation/repassivation is faster but steady-state passive current is higher; the net tribo-corrosion loss is governed by the synergy of wear and corrosion. A partially protective tribo-oxide (Cr- and Al-rich) reduces friction/wear to some extent, but film removal under sliding increases the interaction component at elevated temperature.
recollection.results: Guess: Compared to room temperature, the corrosion current density increases roughly 3–10x with temperature (e.g., icorr ~1–3 µA/cm2 at 25 C to ~10–20 µA/cm2 by ~90–120 C). The total material loss (wear volume) under sliding rises by about 2–3x (e.g., from ~1e-5 to ~2–3e-5 mm3/N·m), and the coefficient of friction remains ~0.45–0.55 with modest temperature dependence. Partitioning of material loss shows the wear–corrosion interaction contributing a majority at high temperature (e.g., ~60–70%). Relative to a reference alloy (e.g., 304 stainless or CoCrMo), the EHEA exhibits lower wear rate and lower/similar icorr at all temperatures due to its hard B2/FCC lamellae and formation of adherent Cr-/Al-rich oxides.

score.note: The recollection identifies elevated-temperature immersed sliding with electrochemical monitoring and approximately the correct temperature range, but omits or hedges key specifics such as the alumina counterbody, thermal-shock cycling, exact loads/frequencies, and DS2205 comparator. It correctly recalls retention of a lamellar dual-phase structure and patchy tribo-oxide formation, but mislabels L12 as generic FCC and adds unsupported selective dissolution and oxide-composition details. The depassivation–repassivation/film-removal competition is broadly correct, yet it misses the crucial minimum-wear polishing regime near 50 °C and incorrectly implies largely monotonic degradation with temperature. The numerical estimates are substantially wrong: actual HEA friction was about 0.18–0.25, wear was lowest at 50 °C rather than rising monotonically, and the cited corrosion-current and synergy values are unsupported.
